chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from some of his companions (I think it is Muhammad ibn Abdillah ibn Hilal or Ali ibn al-Hakam), from al-Ala' ibn Razin, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a man who divorces his wife: when does she become fully divorced (mutallaqah) from him? He said: When the blood of the third menstrual period appears, she gains control of herself. I said: Then is she permitted to marry in that state? He said: Yes, but she should not allow herself to be married until she is purified from the blood.

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: What these narrations encompass is what we act upon, which is that when she sees the blood of the third menstrual period, she gains control of herself and becomes permissible for husbands, and it is valid for her to contract marriage upon herself. However, it is preferable that she delay marriage until she performs the ritual bath (ghusl). If she contracts marriage, she should not allow herself to be married until after the bath. This is the view of al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Sama'ah and Ali ibn Ibrahim ibn Hashim. Ja'far ibn Sama'ah said: She becomes fully divorced upon seeing the blood, except that it is not permissible for her to contract marriage until after the bath. And what we have chosen is more appropriate, and by this our Sheikh (may God have mercy on him) used to issue fatwas. Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) explicitly stated this in the narration of Zurarah, which Umar ibn Udhaynah narrated from him, from his saying: 'And she becomes permissible for husbands.' And the narration which Musa ibn Bakr narrated from Zurarah from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), from his saying: 'And she is not permitted to marry until she bathes from the third menstrual period,' is to be understood as referring to the dislike (karahah) we previously mentioned, that contracting marriage upon her is valid. Muhammad ibn Muslim also narrated it, and we have previously presented the narration from him, and it is mentioned therein that she is not permitted to allow herself to be married until after the bath, according to what we have presented.

key_terms.الْحَيْضَةِ الثَّالِثَةِ: The third menstrual period, used here to determine the duration of the waiting period for a woman divorced during menstruation.
key_terms.الْغُسْلِ: The ritual bath (ghusl) required for purification after menstruation.
key_terms.الْكَرَاهِيَةِ: Dislike (makruh), indicating that while marriage is valid, it is not preferred to contract it before the bath.
key_terms.تَبِينُ: To become fully divorced (mutallaqah), meaning the divorce is complete and the waiting period (iddah) begins.
key_terms.تَمْلِكُ نَفْسَهَا: She gains control of herself, meaning she is no longer in the state of menstruation and her legal status changes.

ai.seo_question: When does a woman divorced during her period become fully eligible for remarriage according to Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfahani's al-Istibsar clarifies the timing of final divorce (talaq al-bayna) for a woman in iddah, establishing that she becomes fully divorced upon the appearance of blood from the third menstrual period. It highlights a key Shia juristic nuance: while the marriage contract (nikah) is technically valid immediately, it is preferred (mustahabb) or conditionally required depending on the scholar (such as al-Shaykh al-Tusi and al-Hassan ibn Muhammad ibn Sam'ah) that she performs ghusl before consummation. The text reconciles differing reports by attributing the 'waiting for ghusl' view to karahat al-tanzihi (dispreferred caution) rather than invalidity.
